excerpt: How long workers' compensation benefits last in Georgia and South Carolina, and what determines when they stop.
keyTakeaways: Workers' comp benefit duration varies by state and disability type: Georgia caps TTD at 400 weeks (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-261) with lifetime benefits for catastrophic injuries; South Carolina allows 500 weeks (S.C. Code § 42-9-10). Medical benefits have no time limit in either state. To maximize benefits, follow your treatment plan, challenge premature MMI declarations, and never accept a settlement without legal review. When benefits end, options include SSDI, third-party lawsuits, and vocational rehabilitation.

faqs.question: What is the maximum time you can receive workers' compensation in Georgia?
faqs.answer: Georgia caps temporary total disability (TTD) at 400 weeks (~7.7 years) under O.C.G.A. § 34-9-261. Temporary partial disability (TPD) is capped at 350 weeks. However, catastrophic injuries — spinal cord injuries, amputations, severe brain injuries, severe burns, or total blindness — qualify for lifetime benefits under O.C.G.A. § 34-9-200.1. Medical benefits have no time limit.

faqs.question: What is the maximum time you can receive workers' compensation in South Carolina?
faqs.answer: South Carolina caps TTD at 500 weeks (~9.6 years) under S.C. Code § 42-9-10, and TPD at 340 weeks. Certain catastrophic injuries may qualify for benefits beyond the standard maximum. Medical benefits continue as long as treatment is reasonable and necessary with no time limit.

faqs.question: Can I receive workers' comp and Social Security disability at the same time?
faqs.answer: Yes, but there is an offset. Federal law limits your combined workers' comp and SSDI benefits to 80% of your pre-injury earnings. If the combined amount exceeds that threshold, your SSDI payment is reduced. An attorney can help structure a workers' comp settlement to minimize the SSDI reduction.

faqs.question: What happens when my workers' comp benefits run out?
faqs.answer: When wage replacement benefits end, your options include: medical benefits (which may continue indefinitely), Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI), Supplemental Security Income (SSI), a personal injury lawsuit if a third party caused your injury, and vocational rehabilitation to retrain for new employment.

faqs.question: Should I accept a lump-sum workers' comp settlement?
faqs.answer: A lump-sum settlement provides guaranteed money but closes out your claim — you generally cannot reopen it for additional benefits later. Never accept a settlement without attorney review. An experienced lawyer can evaluate whether the offer accounts for your future medical needs, remaining disability benefits, and permanent impairment.

faqs.question: How can I prevent the insurer from cutting my benefits short?
faqs.answer: Follow your treatment plan consistently, do not return to work prematurely, get an independent medical opinion if you disagree with the insurer's doctor, challenge premature benefit terminations through a hearing, and hire an attorney early. Insurers use tactics like premature MMI declarations, low impairment ratings, and surveillance to justify ending benefits — legal representation helps counter these strategies.
